In an [earlier post](../2025-05-27-ergm-intuition/index.qmd) I worked through
where ERGM parameter values come from. This post picks up the practical side:
how to fit a model to real network data and how to read the coefficients once
you have them.

The data are advice ties among 47 teachers in an elementary school, along with
a second network of friendship ties among the same teachers. Both are
deidentified. The advice network comes from work on how internal competition
shapes advice seeking in schools. This data are for one of the schools associated with this Public Administration Review piece: https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/puar.12362


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(statnet)
library(texreg)

load("par5.RData")
par5
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
 Network attributes:
  vertices = 18 
  directed = TRUE 
  hyper = FALSE 
  loops = FALSE 
  multiple = FALSE 
  bipartite = FALSE 
  total edges= 71 
    missing edges= 0 
    non-missing edges= 71 

 Vertex attribute names: 
    c.COMP.2 c.EFFIC c.ORG c.PROF COMP.1 COMP.2 EDUC EFFIC GRADE INFL.CLS INFL.SCH INNV INST ORG PROF SCH SOCZ TOT TRTE6 vertex.names YRSDIST 

No edge attributes
```


:::
:::


## Starting with a null model

The simplest possible ERGM says that every tie forms independently, with some
constant probability. In ERGM syntax that is a model with nothing but an
`edges` term.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mod1 <- ergm(par5 ~ edges)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```
Starting maximum pseudolikelihood estimation (MPLE):
```


:::

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```
Obtaining the responsible dyads.
```


:::

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```
Evaluating the predictor and response matrix.
```


:::

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```
Maximizing the pseudolikelihood.
```


:::

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```
Finished MPLE.
```


:::

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```
Evaluating log-likelihood at the estimate. 
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
summary(mod1)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Call:
ergm(formula = par5 ~ edges)

Maximum Likelihood Results:

      Estimate Std. Error MCMC % z value Pr(>|z|)    
edges  -1.1969     0.1354      0  -8.838   <1e-04 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

     Null Deviance: 424.2  on 306  degrees of freedom
 Residual Deviance: 331.5  on 305  degrees of freedom
 
AIC: 333.5  BIC: 337.3  (Smaller is better. MC Std. Err. = 0)
```


:::
:::


The edges coefficient is about $-1.20$. That number is a log-odds, so to get
the probability of a tie we run it back through the inverse logit:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
exp(-1.1969) / (1 + exp(-1.1969))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.2320271
```


:::
:::


Roughly $0.23$. This value is exactly the density of the network:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
gden(par5)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.2320261
```


:::
:::


This is worth sitting with for a moment. In a model where the only thing
governing tie formation is a constant probability, the fitted probability *has*
to be the observed density — there is nothing else in the model to explain
anything. We can confirm the arithmetic directly:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
network.dyadcount(par5)   # 47 * 46 possible directed ties
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 306
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
network.edgecount(par5)   # observed ties
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 71
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
network.edgecount(par5) / network.dyadcount(par5)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.2320261
```


:::
:::


So the null model recovers the density and nothing more. The question is
whether density alone is a good description of this network.

## Simulating from the model

One of the genuinely useful things about ERGMs is that a fitted model is a
probability distribution over networks. We can draw from it and compare what
the model produces against what we actually observed.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sims <- simulate(mod1, nsim = 1)
plot(sims)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Now compare a handful of statistics between the simulated network and the real
one:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
summary(sims ~ edges + mutual + triangle + twopath)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
   edges   mutual triangle  twopath 
      61        6       47      206 
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
summary(par5 ~ edges + mutual + triangle + twopath)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
   edges   mutual triangle  twopath 
      71       19      139      240 
```


:::
:::


The edge counts line up well, which is what we expected — the model was built
to match density. But the observed network has considerably more reciprocated
ties and more triangles than the model produces. Teachers tend to ask *each other* for help, and advice ties cluster into triads. A
model assuming independence between ties has no way to represent either
pattern.

That gap is the whole motivation for everything that follows. We want a model
whose simulated networks look like the one we observed, not just in density but
in the structural features we care about.

## What the statistics actually count

Before adding terms, it helps to see what these network statistics are counting.
The counts are hard to eyeball even in a network of 47 nodes, so here is a toy
undirected network of 7:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
newmat <- rbind(c(0,1,1,1,0,0,0),
                c(1,0,1,1,0,0,0),
                c(1,1,0,1,0,0,0),
                c(1,1,1,0,1,0,0),
                c(0,0,0,1,0,1,1),
                c(0,0,0,0,1,0,1),
                c(0,0,0,0,1,1,0))
newmat <- network(newmat, directed = FALSE)
plot(newmat, displaylabels = TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=672}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
summary(newmat ~ edges + triangle + twopath)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
   edges triangle  twopath 
      10        5       20 
```


:::
:::


And the directed case, where the same three nodes can contribute several
triangles depending on tie direction:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
newmat2 <- rbind(c(0,1,1,0,0,0,0),
                 c(1,0,1,0,0,0,1),
                 c(1,1,0,1,0,1,0),
                 c(0,0,1,0,0,0,0),
                 c(0,0,0,1,0,0,1),
                 c(0,0,0,0,1,0,1),
                 c(0,0,0,0,1,0,0))
newmat2 <- network(newmat2, directed = TRUE)
plot(newmat2, displaylabels = TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=672}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
summary(newmat2 ~ edges + triangle + twopath)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
   edges triangle  twopath 
      15       10       23 
```


:::
:::


Notice that twopaths are nested inside triangles: every triangle contains
twopaths, so the two terms are counting overlapping features of the same edges.
That collinearity is not a nuisance detail — it is a large part of why these
models can be difficult to fit. The estimation has to separate signal among
terms that are structurally entangled with one another.

## Dyadic independent terms

Terms are called *dyadic independent* when the value of one tie does not depend
on any other tie. These behave much like predictors in a logistic regression,
and the interpretation carries over directly.

### Categorical attributes

Teachers in these data either teach a single grade or multiple grades. We can
ask whether that affects the ties they send and receive:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mod2a <- ergm(par5 ~ edges + nodeifactor("GRADE", levels = 8) +
                nodeofactor("GRADE", levels = 8))
```

The coefficient on outgoing ties is about $0.51$. As a log-odds this is not
very interpretable, so exponentiate it:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```
Warning in .Deprecate_once(msg = "Using x$coef to access the coefficient vector

coefficient vector of an ergm is deprecated. Use coef(x) instead.
```


:::

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
nodeofactor.GRADE.Other/Multiple 
                        1.662821 
```


:::

About $1.6$. Holding everything else constant, the odds of sending an advice tie
increase by a factor of roughly 1.6 when the sender teaches multiple grades
rather than one.

It's worth verifying that this is really what the coefficient means. The odds
that a single-grade teacher sends a tie to another single-grade teacher:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

a
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.2101361
```


:::
:::


And for a multiple-grade sender:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
b <- exp(-1.56 + 0.5085)
b
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.3494132
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
b / a
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 1.662795
```


:::
:::


Same $1.66$. Converting to probabilities instead:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
exp(-1.56) / (1 + exp(-1.56))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.1736466
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
exp(-1.56 + 0.5085) / (1 + exp(-1.56 + 0.5085))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.2589372
```


:::
:::


Slightly below and slightly above the overall density, respectively.

### Homophily

A separate question is whether teachers seek advice from others *like*
themselves. `nodematch` tests exactly that:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mod2b <- ergm(par5 ~ edges + nodematch("GRADE", diff = FALSE))
```

```
Maximum Likelihood Results:

                Estimate Std. Error MCMC % z value Pr(>|z|)    
edges            -1.3570     0.1555      0  -8.727   <1e-04 ***
nodematch.GRADE   0.8050     0.3273      0   2.459   0.0139 *  
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

     Null Deviance: 424.2  on 306  degrees of freedom
 Residual Deviance: 325.8  on 304  degrees of freedom
 
AIC: 329.8  BIC: 337.2  (Smaller is better. MC Std. Err. = 0)
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
exp(mod2b$coef[2])
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
nodematch.GRADE 
       2.236597 
```


:::
:::


The odds of a tie between two teachers of the same grade are roughly 2.2 times
the odds of a tie between teachers of different grades. Setting `diff = TRUE`
would estimate a separate homophily parameter for each grade, which is worth
doing when you suspect the tendency varies across categories.

### Another network as a predictor

One of the most useful terms in practice is `edgecov`, which uses a second
network as a dyadic predictor. Here we ask whether friendship predicts advice
seeking.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
load("par.friends.RData")

# confirm the two networks are ordered identically
all(row.names(as.sociomatrix(par.friends)) == row.names(as.sociomatrix(par5)))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] TRUE
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
mod5 <- ergm(par5 ~ edges + edgecov(par.friends))
```

```
Maximum Likelihood Results:

                    Estimate Std. Error MCMC % z value Pr(>|z|)    
edges                -2.9704     0.3625      0  -8.194   <1e-04 ***
edgecov.par.friends   2.7441     0.3999      0   6.862   <1e-04 ***

     Null Deviance: 424.2  on 306  degrees of freedom
 Residual Deviance: 259.0  on 304  degrees of freedom
 
AIC: 263  BIC: 270.4  (Smaller is better. MC Std. Err. = 0)
```

```{.r .cell-code}
exp(mod5$coef[2])
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
edgecov.par.friends 
           15.55063 
```


:::
:::


Advice ties are roughly 15 times more likely between teachers who are also
friends. That row-name check above matters more than it looks — if the two
networks are ordered differently, `edgecov` will silently compare the wrong
dyads and hand you a plausible, wrong answer.

## Where this leaves us

Everything so far assumes ties are independent of one another given the
covariates. That assumption is what makes these models straightforward to fit
and interpret — and it is also what the earlier simulation showed to be wrong.
The excess reciprocity and clustering in the observed network are precisely the
patterns dyadic independent terms cannot capture.

[The next post](../2026-08-09-ergm-interpretation_part2/index.qmd) takes up dyadic
dependent terms along with the model degeneracy, and how to
check whether a fitted model actually reproduces the network you started with.
